subtopic: Operator fusion / Vertical vs. horizontal vs. epilogue
learningObjective: Distinguish vertical (producer-consumer) fusion, horizontal fusion, and epilogue fusion by their data-flow patterns.
stem: In deep-learning compilers, three commonly discussed fusion patterns are 'vertical', 'horizontal', and 'epilogue' fusion. Which description matches all three correctly?

options.text: Vertical fusion merges a producer with its consumer along the data-flow edge; horizontal fusion merges independent operators that share the same input or launch dimensions; epilogue fusion attaches a lightweight elementwise op onto the tail of a heavy compute op such as GEMM.

Vertical fusion means merging operators executed on different devices; horizontal fusion means merging operators of the same type across the batch dimension; epilogue fusion means merging the backward pass into the forward pass.
All three refer to launching multiple CUDA kernels concurrently on separate streams; the names only differ by which kernel finishes first in the timeline.
Vertical fusion is loop-level fusion of nested loops; horizontal fusion is basic-block CSE within a single operator; epilogue fusion is compile-time constant folding of the final output.

explanation: Vertical (producer-consumer) fusion combines an op with its data-flow consumer so the intermediate tensor is kept in registers/shared memory instead of DRAM. Horizontal fusion combines independent ops sharing a launch dimension (e.g., three sibling elementwise ops on the same tensor) into one kernel to amortize launch overhead. Epilogue fusion fuses a small pointwise op (bias-add, activation, scaling) into the tail of a compute-heavy op like GEMM/Conv, reusing the accumulator without an extra DRAM round-trip.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: matches the standard definitions used across TVM, TorchInductor, XLA, and cuBLAS epilogues.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: cross-device merge is not fusion; forward-backward merging is not epilogue fusion.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: concurrent-stream launching is not fusion at all — fusion is a single-kernel construction.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: conflates fusion with unrelated optimizations (CSE, constant folding, loop nesting).

assumptions: The three names are used in their standard compiler-community sense.
nonImplications: Does not imply any of the three fusion kinds is always beneficial; each has legality and performance preconditions.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses fusion with placement / autograd concepts.
distractorRationales.D: Confuses fusion with CSE / constant folding.
